items.passage: Darius came down to the harbor every Thursday, though he claimed he only wanted the air. I told him the air smelled of diesel and gutted mullet, and he agreed and stayed anyway. We mended nets side by side. He asked about my knees, my brother's boat, the price of ice. He never asked why I had stopped coming to the church on the hill, and I never offered. Once a boy ran past shouting that the bells were being repaired, and Darius bent lower over the knot he was tying until the boy was gone. I complained, as always, that he worked too slowly and wasted good twine. Still, on the Thursday he was ill, I left the end of the net unfinished, folded it over the bollard where he usually sat, and went home early. When he returned, he found the frayed corner waiting and said nothing about it, only threaded his needle and began where he had stopped.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Darius?
options: Resentful of Darius's repeated efforts to draw him back to the hill church
Indifferent to Darius's company, which he tolerates only out of habit
Quietly appreciative of Darius's restraint, despite routine complaints
Amused by Darius's clumsiness with the nets and the wasted twine
items.explanation: 화자는 Darius가 교회 이야기를 한 번도 꺼내지 않고, 종 수리 소식에도 고개를 숙여 화제를 피해 준다는 점을 반복해 보여 준다. 화자는 느리다고 불평하지만 Darius가 아픈 날 그물 끝을 그의 자리에 남겨 두어 그를 기다렸음을 행동으로 드러낸다. 따라서 겉의 불평 아래 그의 절제에 대한 조용한 고마움이 있다는 C가 정답이다. A는 Darius가 오히려 교회 이야기를 피한다는 점과 맞지 않고, B와 D는 그물을 남겨 둔 행동이 보여 주는 애착을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: When the fog came in off the Cornish water, Jonah lit the second lamp in the workshop and bent again over the ledger he was binding. Nargis had come to speak of her grandmother, who could no longer manage the stairs of the cottage above. She had rehearsed the English words on the walk from the station, plain and reasonable: a room in town, a nurse, a window on the square. Jonah heard her out, then showed her how the old woman had once taught him to pare leather so thin the light came through it. Nargis took the knife, as she had when she was a child, and pared badly. Later, gathering her coat, she noticed that he had set aside a strip of the finest calfskin, labelled in her grandmother's hand, which he had never once used. She said she would write to the nurse on Monday, and she buttoned her coat slowly, and she did not take the strip away from his bench.
items.question: Which choice best describes Nargis's attitude toward Jonah as presented in the passage?
options: Impatient with Jonah's refusal to discuss the matter in plain, simple English
Contemptuous of Jonah's devotion to an old-fashioned and dying craft
Persuaded by Jonah's lesson to abandon her plan for the grandmother
Resolved on her plan yet gentle toward Jonah's attachment to the past
items.explanation: Nargis는 준비해 온 계획을 끝까지 유지해 월요일에 간호인에게 편지를 쓰겠다고 말하므로 계획을 포기하지 않는다. 동시에 아버지가 건넨 칼을 어릴 때처럼 받아 들고, 할머니 글씨가 붙은 가죽 조각을 그대로 두며 단추를 천천히 채우는 행동에서 아버지의 애착을 존중하는 태도가 드러난다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. C는 그녀가 계획을 그대로 진행한다는 점과 충돌하고, A와 B는 지문에 근거가 없는 적대감을 가정한다.

items.passage:
Years later I still see the depot at dawn,
the number 9 coughing its blue breath into the fog,
and my uncle Shuang holding out a paper cup of soy milk
the morning after I told him I could not pay.

He said nothing of the money.
He asked if my shoes were warm.

I drank it, and I counted the coins in my pocket
the whole ride into Chengdu, as if they might have multiplied.

My mother said he was buying patience.
My cousin said he was buying me.
I said nothing, Haneul who always says nothing,
and kept the cup, which I still have,
which I have never washed and never thrown away.

Some mornings I lift it to the window
and turn it, looking for the price printed on the bottom,
and find only the depot's faded name.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward the uncle's gift of soy milk?
options: Unsettled, cherishing the gesture while still questioning its motive
Grateful, having concluded that the uncle's kindness was entirely selfless
Bitter, convinced the uncle used the soy milk to control him
Detached, recalling the depot only as a backdrop to his commute
items.explanation: 화자는 컵을 씻지도 버리지도 않고 지금까지 간직해 선물을 소중히 여긴다는 점을 보여 준다. 그러나 동전을 세던 장면과 컵 바닥에서 '가격'을 찾는 행동은 그 친절에 대가가 있었는지 여전히 의심한다는 뜻이다. 어머니와 사촌의 해석 사이에서 화자는 아무 말도 하지 않아 판단을 보류한다. 따라서 A가 정답이며, B와 C는 화자가 내리지 않은 결론을 한쪽으로 확정하고 D는 컵에 대한 애착을 무시한다.

items.passage: Smell of wet ink and wool sacking filled the post office the winter I practiced my recitation there, because it was the only building on our stretch of the plateau with a stove that stayed lit. Tallulah, who sorted the mail and had once ridden with my father, listened from behind the grille. I told her that she corrected my pauses too often and that my father would have let me speak at my own pace. She only nodded and went on stamping letters. On the evening before the program, however, I arrived early and found her chair turned to face the bench where I stood, and I recited the whole piece to it before she came in. When she did, I began again from the first line, slower this time, waiting at each pause for the small tap of her pencil against the counter.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Tallulah?
options: Openly hostile toward Tallulah, whom she blames for her father's absence
Outwardly impatient with Tallulah but quietly reliant on her guidance
Largely indifferent to Tallulah, valuing only the warmth of the stove
Admiring of Tallulah chiefly for her past travels with the father
items.explanation: 화자는 Tallulah가 쉼표를 너무 자주 고친다고 불평하며 아버지와 비교해 겉으로는 짜증을 드러낸다. 하지만 공연 전날 그녀의 의자를 향해 먼저 낭송하고, 그녀가 오자 처음부터 다시 천천히 하며 연필 두드림을 기다린다. 이는 그녀의 지도에 기대고 있음을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A는 지문에 없는 원망을 가정하고, C는 의자를 향한 행동을 설명하지 못하며, D는 아버지와의 과거만 근거로 삼는다.

items.passage: Tromso in March was all slush and salt, and you pushed your mother's chair three streets to Soren's shop because she would let no one else cut her hair. Soren worked in silence, as he always had, the scissors ticking like a clock under the mirror. Halfway through, your mother said she was sorry for the years she had not written, for the wedding she had not attended. You told her the wind had been loud and asked her to repeat it, and when she did, you asked Soren whether the back should be shorter. Afterward you brushed the cut hair from her collar with your own glove, carefully, the way she had once brushed snow from yours. On the walk home you named the shops you passed, one by one, until the door.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the mother in the passage?
options: Openly forgiving, eager to accept the apology and move past old hurts
Coldly resentful, performing each duty mainly to shame the mother
Tenderly attentive, yet unwilling to take up the mother's apology
Mildly bored, more interested in the barbershop than the mother
items.explanation: 화자는 어머니의 사과를 바람 탓으로 못 들은 척하고, 다시 듣자 곧바로 머리 길이 이야기로 화제를 돌려 사과를 받아들이지 않는다. 그러나 장갑으로 옷깃의 머리카락을 조심스럽게 털어 주는 행동은 깊은 보살핌을 보여 준다. 따라서 다정하게 돌보면서도 사과에는 응하지 않는 C가 정답이다. A는 회피 행동과 맞지 않고, B와 D는 조심스러운 돌봄의 장면을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: “You take the kitchen, I'll take the garden plot,” Itzel said, laying the keys on the bench between the bean rows. Milena agreed too quickly, and for an hour the twins sorted the contents of their mother's house aloud: two kettles, one clock, a drawer of mismatched string. Every Sunday for eleven years they had come to this plot in Gdansk to water the tomatoes she had planted. Neither of them, Milena admitted while coiling the hose, had ever liked tomatoes. Itzel laughed and said she had always given hers to the neighbors. They went on listing furniture, assigning it, trading it back. At six, when the sprinklers in the other plots began to hiss, both of them reached for the same watering can, and Milena let go first, and then Itzel handed it back, and they filled it together at the tap.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?
options: To recount how the twins divided their mother's furniture and goods
To suggest that family duties are usually kept up without any real pleasure
To show that a shared watering can is a family's most valued object
To show that dividing the house cannot divide the ritual the twins share
items.explanation: 지문은 집과 물건을 나누는 장면으로 시작하지만, 중간에 두 사람 모두 토마토를 좋아하지 않았다는 고백으로 물주기가 맛 때문이 아니라 둘을 잇는 의식이었음을 드러낸다. 끝에서 같은 물뿌리개를 동시에 잡고 함께 물을 채우는 장면은 그 의식이 분할 뒤에도 남는다는 것을 보여 준다. 세 곳을 모두 아우르는 D가 정답이다. A는 처음 일화만, B는 중간 고백만 일반화했고, C는 마지막 사물을 과장해 요지로 삼았다.

items.passage: We called it the salt pool, though by Bartolo's ninth summer in Havana the sea had long since cracked its seaward wall. Each morning Dario sat on the edge with his trousers rolled and named things for her in the old language: tile, gull, the green rust on the ladder. She repeated each word and swam a length between words. On Thursday she stopped halfway, clung to the rope, and climbed out by the near ladder, saying the water was too cold. Dario, who had seen everything, said only that cold had two words, one for water and one for people, and made her practice both. She did not tell him she had wanted to reach the far wall before her mother arrived. He did not tell her he had noticed. When they walked home, she carried his towel, and he carried the word for rope, saying it over to himself.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?
options: To show how a language lesson lets the two quietly protect each other's pride
To describe a daily routine of swimming lessons in a crumbling Havana pool
To argue that every language holds separate words for physical and emotional cold
To suggest that Dario is slowly losing his memory of the language he teaches
items.explanation: 처음에는 단어를 배우며 수영하는 일상이 제시되고, 중간에 Bartolo가 실패를 추위 탓으로 돌리자 Dario가 알면서도 '추위'의 두 단어로 수업을 이어 간다. 이어 서로 말하지 않은 사실이 대칭으로 놓이고, 마지막에 그가 '밧줄'이라는 단어를 되뇌는 장면은 그 실패를 조용히 기억하고 있음을 암시한다. 따라서 언어 수업을 통해 두 사람이 서로의 자존심을 지켜 준다는 A가 정답이다. B는 처음 일화만, C는 중간 진술만 일반화했고, D는 마지막 장면을 기억 상실로 과장했다.

items.passage: A tin of cardamom sat on the boarding-house counter in Haifa for three nights before Emiliano understood it had come back to him. He had left it at Rivka's door after their shift at the bakery, a small thanks for covering his hours when his son was ill. Now it stood beside the kettle, unopened, with a note in her square handwriting: keep this for your boy. Emiliano took it as a refusal, and for a week he made his coffee plain and spoke to her only about ovens. Yet Rivka had grown up in a house where a gift returned was a gift doubled, a way of saying the debt ran in both directions. Neither of them knew the other's rule. On the eighth night she brewed coffee with cardamom from her own jar and left a cup beside his, which he drank, slowly, standing by the window.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?
options: To recount how Emiliano thanked Rivka for covering his night hours at the bakery
To show how differing customs strain, then quietly mend, a working friendship
To argue that returning a gift is generally a sign of greater generosity
To suggest that shared coffee is the true foundation of their friendship
items.explanation: 처음 일화에서 감사의 선물이 되돌아오자 Emiliano는 이를 거절로 받아들여 거리를 둔다. 중간의 'Yet' 문장은 Rivka의 집안에서는 선물을 돌려주는 것이 오히려 호의였다는 반전을 제시하고, 끝에서 그녀가 카다몸 커피를 건네며 관계가 회복된다. 세 부분을 모두 포괄하는 B가 정답이다. A는 처음 일화만, C는 중간 진술을 일반 원리로 확대했으며, D는 마지막 커피 장면을 과장했다.

items.passage: Wool remembers every hand. Aster had said so to the cooperative in Cape Town on the morning Kagiso, who had bought the old house and its looms, tangled a warp before thirty weavers and the visiting buyers. Kagiso laughed too loudly and left the shed. That evening Aster, who also kept the garden behind the house, found her among the lemon trees and said nothing about looms; she asked instead which beds should be turned for winter. Kagiso, to her own surprise, knew. Her grandmother had grown lemons in Mafikeng, and she named the soil and the pruning months without stopping. Aster listened as if being taught. In the following week Kagiso came to the shed each dawn, before the others, and Aster left a single spool beside her bench, already wound, its loose end tucked under so that it would not unravel.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?
options: To recount how Kagiso tangled a warp before the whole cooperative and its buyers
To argue that skill in gardening usually leads to skill in weaving
To show how Aster restores Kagiso's confidence by first letting her teach
To suggest that a single wound spool repaired the entire cooperative
items.explanation: 처음 일화는 Kagiso가 사람들 앞에서 실수해 당황하는 장면이고, 중간에 Aster는 베틀 대신 정원 이야기를 꺼내 Kagiso가 아는 것을 말하게 하며 배우는 사람처럼 듣는다. 끝에서 Aster가 미리 감아 둔 실패를 놓아 두는 행동은 다시 시작하려는 Kagiso를 조용히 돕는다는 뜻이다. 세 곳을 모두 아우르는 C가 정답이다. A는 처음 일화만, B는 중간 장면을 잘못 일반화했으며, D는 마지막 사물을 과장했다.

items.passage: Once, near the end of my nights at the pharmacy in Lima, Valentina came in at two in the morning and did not ask for anything on the shelves. For six years she had sent me her chapters typed, never handwritten; the notebooks she kept locked in a drawer her own sister had never seen. That week a colleague had told me, kindly and wrongly, that Valentina was talking to a translator in Madrid. I said as much while I rang up the mints she finally chose. She looked at the fluorescent tubes and remarked that they made everyone look like a ghost of themselves. Then she set a green notebook on the counter, its pages crowded with her slanted ink and crossed-out lines, and said she would collect it Thursday. I put it under the register, beside the night ledger, and kept my hand on its cover until the bell over the door stopped swinging.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Valentina most likely leave the notebook with the narrator?
options: She wants the narrator to hide her private notebooks from her sister
She means to show her trust in the narrator without answering the rumor aloud
She is too embarrassed by the rumor to discuss her writing at all
She intends to hand over a final draft before she leaves Lima for Madrid at last
items.explanation: 앞부분은 Valentina가 손으로 쓴 공책을 누구에게도, 심지어 자매에게도 보여 주지 않았다는 습관을 알려 준다. 중간에 화자가 소문을 꺼내자 그녀는 형광등 이야기로 말을 돌려 소문에 직접 답하지 않는다. 그 직후 가장 사적인 공책을 맡기는 행동은 말 대신 신뢰를 보여 주려는 것이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 앞 단서만 빌렸고, C는 회피만 설명하며 공책을 건넨 행동과 충돌하고, D는 '마드리드'라는 표현을 빌렸지만 소문이 틀렸다는 서술과 모순된다.

items.passage: “Walk me to the railing, if you are not too tired,” Ofelia said, though the doctor had forbidden the night air. I wheeled her along the promenade at Valparaiso, as I had each evening that month, and she counted the lamps aloud, as she always did, never once losing the number. That afternoon I had found, among her blankets, a letter addressed to her son in Santiago, unsealed and plainly unfinished. When I mentioned that the post left at dawn, she asked whether the gulls ever slept, and whether I had a son myself. At the railing she held out the letter and asked me to read it to her, slowly, every line. I read it. She corrected two words, made me read it again, and then folded it into my apron pocket and turned her chair, without my help, toward the lamps.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Ofelia most likely ask the narrator to read the letter aloud?
options: She doubts her own memory and needs help recalling what she wrote
She wishes to keep the letter's contents secret from her son
She wants the letter sent but cannot bear to send it by herself
She is testing whether the nurse has already read her private letter
items.explanation: Ofelia는 가로등 수를 한 번도 틀리지 않고 세며 편지의 두 단어를 직접 고칠 만큼 정신이 또렷하다. 그런데 우체국 이야기가 나오자 갈매기 이야기로 말을 돌려 스스로 편지를 부치는 일을 피한다. 결국 편지를 다듬은 뒤 간호사의 앞치마 주머니에 넣어 주므로, 편지가 전해지기를 바라면서도 혼자서는 보내지 못한다는 C가 정답이다. A는 또렷한 기억력과 충돌하고, B는 편지를 맡긴 행동과 모순되며, D는 지문에 근거가 없다.

items.passage: Three rules governed the noodle stall near the Kamo River in Kyoto: pay first, eat standing, and never keep the cook waiting. None of them was broken the night you found Mattie there, your old teacher, drinking broth beside the lantern as if she had been waiting a decade. For years you had kept her class photograph face down in a drawer, because in it you stood at the edge, half cut off by the frame. She asked about your work, and you answered with the price of the noodles in yen and dollars and then in the coins of your childhood. When she took a photograph from her own coat, the same one, you saw that she had trimmed it with scissors so that you stood in the center. You bought her a second bowl, though she had not finished the first, and you stood beside her until the cook put out the lantern.
items.question: Based on the passage, why do you most likely buy Mattie a second bowl?
options: To repay Mattie for once having cut you out of the class photograph
To follow the stall's rule against keeping the cook waiting for orders
To avoid discussing your work by keeping the teacher busy eating
To stay near a teacher who, you learn, had kept you at the center
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 '당신'은 사진 가장자리에 잘려 있다는 이유로 그 사진을 오래 뒤집어 두었고, 이는 선생님에게 주변적인 존재였다고 느꼈음을 암시한다. 중간에서는 일에 대한 질문을 국수 값 이야기로 피하며 거리를 둔다. 그러나 선생님이 자신을 가운데에 두도록 사진을 잘라 간직했음을 알게 된 직후 두 번째 그릇을 사므로, 그 곁에 머물고 싶다는 D가 정답이다. A는 사진 단서를 거꾸로 읽었고, B는 규칙 표현만 빌렸으며, C는 회피 단서만 설명한다.

items.passage: Haruto has already taken the better chair when you arrive at the tailor's back room in Addis Ababa, so you take the stool by the bolts of cotton and say good morning as if you meant it. You and he have baked on the same street for nine years. The rule, written by no one, is that neither of you sells bread before seven; the market council has called you both to decide whether it still holds now that the bus station has moved. Lindiwe, the tailor, pours tea and leaves you to it. Haruto compliments your new ovens. You compliment his sign. He stirs his tea long after the sugar has gone, and you count the pins in the cushion beside you: forty, forty-one. When the clerk finally arrives, the two of you rise at the same moment, and each holds the curtain open for the other until it slips from both your hands.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?
options: Courteous on the surface, yet tense with a rivalry neither will voice
Calm and relaxed, reflecting an easy friendship between neighbors
Openly hostile, as each baker tries to humiliate the other aloud
Anxious at first, then fully at ease once the council clerk finally arrives
items.explanation: 두 제빵사는 인사와 칭찬을 주고받으며 겉으로는 예의 바르다. 그러나 좋은 의자를 먼저 차지하는 행동, 설탕이 녹은 뒤에도 차를 젓고 핀을 세는 행동은 말하지 않은 긴장을 보여 준다. 마지막에 서로 커튼을 붙잡아 주다 놓치는 장면도 양보 경쟁을 드러내므로 A가 정답이다. B는 겉 정서만 반영했고, C는 속 긴장을 과장했으며, D는 지문에 없는 마지막의 해소로 어조를 고정했다.

items.passage: When Weiqi climbed up to the roof the first evening back, I was already sitting against the water tank, pretending to read. Taipei hummed below us, scooters and rain on tin, and she said the view had not changed, which was untrue; three new towers stood where the night market had been. I said it was nice of her to visit. “Yuxuan, I didn't visit,” she said. “I moved back.” For a while we talked about her new school, the price of mangoes, my brother's motorbike, and I laughed at the right places. Then she set her old key ring on the rim of the tank, the one with the plastic cat I had given her the summer she left without saying goodbye. I did not pick it up. I did not push it away either, and when the rain grew heavier, I moved a little to make room for her under the overhang.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?
options: Breezy and carefree, like any pleasant reunion between old friends
Casual on the surface, beneath which a guarded hurt slowly softens
Bitterly accusatory, as the narrator punishes Weiqi for leaving
Coolly guarded throughout, with no change at all in the narrator's stance
items.explanation: 두 사람은 학교와 망고 값 같은 가벼운 이야기를 나누고 화자는 적절한 곳에서 웃어 겉으로는 편안하다. 그러나 책을 읽는 척하는 모습과 '방문'이라는 거리 두는 말, 열쇠고리를 집지 않는 행동은 작별 없이 떠난 데 대한 상처를 보여 준다. 마지막에 비를 피할 자리를 내주는 행동은 그 경계가 조금씩 풀린다는 뜻이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 겉 정서만, C는 속 감정을 과장했고, D는 마지막의 변화를 무시했다.

items.passage: Years later, Larissa would describe that week as a matter of logistics. The guesthouse beside the old monastery in Lisbon was being sold, and she and Caio, who had shared its thin middle wall for twenty years, were the last tenants to clear their rooms. She labeled boxes. She rented a van. She told Caio, briskly, that the brass coat hook between their two doors belonged to neither of them and should stay for the buyers. Caio agreed. Yet on the final morning he found her on the landing with a screwdriver, loosening the hook's screws one quarter turn at a time, and then tightening them again. Neither of them mentioned it. They carried the last chair down together, and the hook stayed on the wall, a pale outline around it where twenty winters of coats had kept the paint from fading.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?
options: Efficient and businesslike, focused entirely on finishing the move
Openly mournful, dwelling at length on the sorrow of leaving home
Brisk and practical in manner, yet threaded with reluctant grief
Detached at first but finally joyful once the last chair is moved
items.explanation: 짧은 문장으로 상자에 이름을 붙이고 차를 빌리는 장면은 사무적이고 빠른 겉모습을 만든다. 그러나 마지막 날 Larissa가 옷걸이 나사를 풀었다 다시 조이는 행동과, 옷걸이 주변의 바래지 않은 자국 묘사는 떠나기 아쉬운 슬픔을 드러낸다. 겉과 속을 함께 아우르는 C가 정답이다. A는 겉 정서만, B는 슬픔을 과장했으며, D는 지문에 없는 기쁨으로 어조를 바꿨다.

items.passage: Bees do not forgive clumsiness. Orla had said so the first spring Paloma rented the cottage behind her yard in Riga, and for eleven years after, the two women spoke mostly through notes about rent and the sagging gate. Paloma signed hers with her full name and the date. Orla signed hers with a single initial. This morning a hive swarmed onto the fence between them, and Orla, her veil torn, stood very still. Paloma crossed the yard with her own veil in her hand and said, “Orla, put this on,” as if she had always used the name. Orla put it on. Afterward, when the swarm had been coaxed into a fresh box, Orla carried the only bench out of the shed and set it on Paloma's side of the fence, then sat on an overturned bucket beside it and handed her the smoker to hold.
items.question: Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Orla and Paloma?
options: Paloma resents Orla's authority as landlord and seeks to embarrass her
They share a strictly businesslike bond, polite but without warmth
Orla shelters a helpless Paloma, who depends entirely on her beekeeping expertise
Their long formality hides a mutual regard that both now begin to show
items.explanation: 두 사람은 11년 동안 집세 쪽지로만 소통했지만, Paloma가 처음으로 'Orla'라고 이름을 부르며 자기 베일을 건네는 순간 호칭이 바뀐다. Orla 역시 하나뿐인 의자를 Paloma 쪽에 놓고 자신은 양동이에 앉아 훈연기를 맡기며 존중을 행동으로 보인다. 두 단서를 모두 설명하는 D가 정답이다. B는 표면의 사무적 태도만 보았고, C는 도움의 방향을 뒤집었으며, A는 지문에 근거가 없다.

items.passage: Shanghai had flooded again, and by midnight the water in the clinic's cellar reached my knees. Meilin had sent for me, not for the pumps, and I came, as I always do when she sends. She called me Mayor at the top of the stairs, as she does in front of the council, and handed me the lamp without asking. I held it while she lifted crates of vaccine onto the shelves, and I did not mention the winter she had sat three nights beside my father when no other doctor would come. She did not mention the clinic's lease, which I have renewed each year without a fee. When the last crate was dry, she took the higher step and offered me her hand, and I took it, and on the way up she said my name, just Gil, and told me to mind the loose board.
items.question: Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between the narrator and Meilin?
options: Bound by unspoken debts, they show loyalty through acts rather than words
Meilin treats Gil with stiff formality because she quietly distrusts his office
Gil commands Meilin, who obeys him because she depends on his lease
Meilin feels indebted to Gil, while he believes he owes her nothing
items.explanation: Gil은 Meilin이 아버지 곁을 지켜 준 일을 말하지 않고, Meilin은 무료로 갱신되는 임대 계약을 말하지 않아 서로의 빚이 양방향임을 보여 준다. 대신 Gil은 부르면 언제나 와서 등불을 들고, Meilin은 손을 내밀며 마지막에 이름을 불러 행동으로 유대를 드러낸다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 'Mayor'라는 표면적 호칭만 보았고, C는 한 단서만 근거로 권력 관계를 만들었으며, D는 빚의 방향을 한쪽으로 뒤집었다.

items.passage: “Somebody could have signed the form,” Leah said, before Colby had even hung up his coat. The customs post at the Ohio rail yard had lost its chance at the federal contract that morning, and everyone in the cramped office knew the paperwork had arrived a day late. Colby, who had trained her for two years, said only that the coffee was burnt again. He poured himself a cup anyway. Leah went on sorting manifests, slapping each one down harder than the last. Around noon a freight inspector asked who was responsible for the missing signature, and Colby answered before she could: the delay was his, he said, an old man's forgetting. Leah stopped sorting. When the inspector left, she took the burnt coffee from Colby's desk, poured it out, and set a fresh pot going without a word.
items.question: Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Leah and Colby?
options: Colby resents Leah for costing the office its federal contract
Leah's anger gives way to grateful regard as Colby shields her
The two keep a cordial, professional distance throughout the day
Leah defers to Colby only because he is the senior officer
items.explanation: 처음에 Leah는 Colby를 탓하는 말을 던지고 서류를 거칠게 내려놓으며 분노를 드러낸다. 그러나 Colby가 조사관 앞에서 책임을 자신에게 돌리자 그녀는 손을 멈추고, 그가 참고 마시던 탄 커피를 버린 뒤 새로 끓인다. 이 두 단서는 원망이 그를 보호해 준 데 대한 고마움으로 바뀌었음을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A는 원망의 방향을 뒤집었고, C는 표면의 사무적 태도만 보았으며, D는 서열이라는 한 측면만 근거로 삼았다.

items.passage: Two rules held on Birdie's barge: no singing after dark, and no one touches the lantern on the stern. I kept both the summer I stayed with her on the river outside Thessaloniki, though I had sung beside her for six seasons in the music halls, and though the lantern, cracked and blackened, had once hung over our stage. Birdie trimmed its wick every evening and never lit it. Her niece, who was seven, asked me one night why we had stopped singing together. I told her our voices had grown tired. The child looked at the lantern and asked why, then, Aunt Birdie still cleaned it. Neither of us answered. Later, when the girl was asleep, Birdie took a match from her apron, struck it, and held it near the wick until the flame reached her fingers and went out.
items.question: In the passage, the lantern on the stern most likely represents
options: Birdie's wish to forbid all singing aboard the barge once darkness falls
the danger that river travel poses to anyone careless with fire
the shared past on stage that neither woman can relight or discard
the niece's curiosity about the adults' lives before the river
items.explanation: 등불은 두 사람이 함께 서던 무대 위에 걸려 있던 물건이며, Birdie는 매일 심지를 다듬으면서도 불을 켜지 않는다. 아이가 왜 아직 등불을 닦느냐고 묻자 두 사람 모두 대답하지 못해, 목소리가 지쳤다는 화자의 설명이 회피였음이 드러난다. 마지막에 불을 붙이려다 끝내 꺼지게 두는 행동은 버리지도 되살리지도 못하는 과거를 보여 주므로 C가 정답이다. A는 규칙을 문자 그대로 읽었고, B는 지문에 근거가 없으며, D는 등불이 아니라 아이의 질문에 초점을 둔다.

items.passage: Once each spring, for as long as either of us could remember, Layla and I rented the same farmhouse beyond the walls of Marrakesh, and once each spring we said perhaps twenty words to each other. That year the grafted orange tree by the well bore fruit for the first time. Layla had cut and bound its branch four springs before, with twine and a paste of clay, and had told no one. When the farmer's wife praised the oranges, Layla shrugged and said the tree had simply been lucky. Yet each morning I saw her walk the long way to the well, past the tree, and touch the scar where the branch had joined, as one touches a sleeping child's forehead. On our last evening she set a single orange on my windowsill, unpeeled, with a length of twine still knotted around its stem.
items.question: In the passage, the grafted orange tree most likely represents
options: the farmer's wife's admiration for the farmhouse orchard
the good luck that Layla claims alone produced the fruit
the narrator's envy of Layla's skill with plants and trees
Layla's hidden pride in a patient work she will not claim
items.explanation: Layla는 4년 전 직접 가지를 접붙였지만 아무에게도 말하지 않았고, 칭찬을 받자 운이 좋았을 뿐이라며 어깨를 으쓱한다. 그러나 매일 아침 일부러 먼 길로 돌아가 접붙인 자리를 아이 이마 만지듯 쓰다듬는 행동은 숨긴 자부심을 드러낸다. 따라서 나무는 내세우지 않는 인내의 결실에 대한 자부심을 상징하며 D가 정답이다. B는 Layla의 겉말을 그대로 믿은 오독이고, A와 C는 지문에 근거가 약한 인물의 감정을 끌어온다.
